title: Yalta, wife of Rav Nachman
author: Aharon Hyman
attribution: Model-assisted translation, editorially reviewed; publication authorized by Joshua Waxman.

paragraphs: Hyman writes that he has already explained in the entry on Rav Nachman that it is very likely to say that she was the daughter of Rabbah bar Avuha, and that her father Rabbah bar Avuha was from the house of the Nesi'im (the exilarchic family), as is explained in the letter of Rav Sherira Gaon, part 2, chapter 3, and that Rav Nachman, a student of her father, married her. (And in the Sheiltot, Vayera, end of section 63: it is proven that she married Rav Nachman when she was a widow or divorcee; see there in the commentary of our master the Gaon, the Netziv.)

She is mentioned several times in the Talmud, as in Berakhot 51b, where she became angry at Ulla and sent him the message: "From peddlers, words; and from rags, lice," and she broke four hundred jars of wine.
And in Gittin 63b, that she made a remedy for Rav Amram the Pious.
And in Kiddushin 70b, when Rav Yehuda came to Rav Nachman, she sent to him: "Settle his dispute, lest he make you like other ignoramuses."
And in Chullin 109b, she asked Rav Nachman: "Since all that the Merciful One forbade us..." etc.
And in Niddah 20b, that she brought blood to Rabbah bar bar Chana, who declared it impure for her; she then came to Rav Yitzchak son of Rav Yehuda, who declared it pure for her.

notes.text: Rabbah bar Avuha, her proposed father, is the person to whom Hyman attributes descent from the house of the Nesi'im (the exilarchic family). In the fuller Niddah account Yalta brings the blood to Rabbah bar bar Chana and then to Rav Yitzchak. The source here has איתתא, while the fuller passage uses אייתא/אייתאי (“brought”).

The locally retained Oxford 1888 Epistle, question 1 paragraph 71, names Rabbah bar Avuha’s house of the Nesi’im; the accompanying Landau 1904 French explicitly calls it the exilarchic family. This supports the institutional sense, not Yalta’s proposed parentage or Hyman’s exact part 2 chapter 3 numbering. The inspected Niddah 20b confirms the two blood rulings and ultimately says Yitzchak relied on his own tradition.
